historical_references.reference: Muhtasibs were high-ranking officials in the Islamic world responsible for maintaining order and enforcing market regulations in the markets and public places.
historical_references.context: The term 'Muhtasib' comes from the Arabic word 'muhasib', which means 'examiner' or 'inspector'. Muhtasibs were first mentioned in the 7th century in the city of Damascus under the Umayyad caliphate. They were tasked with ensuring fair trade practices, maintaining public order, and enforcing moral codes. The role of the Muhtasib continued to evolve throughout the Islamic world, with the position reaching its peak during the Abbasid caliphate in the 13th and 14th centuries.

historical_references.reference: Another notable figure with the title 'Muhtasim' was the Abbasid caliph al-Muhtasim bi-llah (r. 868-870), who is known for his patronage of art and architecture.
historical_references.context: Al-Muhtasim bi-llah was the fifth caliph of the Abbasid caliphate and is considered one of the most influential rulers of the period. He is known for his patronage of the arts, particularly his support for Persian influence in Islamic art and architecture. He built several notable structures, including the Great Mosque of Kufa and the Mosque of al-Khadra in Baghdad.
